name: Fabio Investment Lab
sources: DeMiguel, Garlappi & Uppal: Optimal versus naive diversification (2009)
Brunnermeier, Nagel & Pedersen: Carry trades and currency crashes (2008/2009)
Gorton & Rouwenhorst: Facts and fantasies about commodity futures (2004 working paper)
Liu & Tsyvinski: Risks and returns of cryptocurrency (2018)
Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen: Time series momentum (2012)
US copper proclamation: product scope and timing

pitches.name: Novo Nordisk
pitches.headline: A capacity-constrained growth franchise with a price-sensitive thesis.
pitches.facts: H1 2024 sales were DKK 133.4bn, up 25% at constant exchange rates. Operating profit was DKK 57.8bn, including a DKK 5.7bn ocedurenone impairment. Obesity-care sales grew 37% at constant exchange rates. These figures establish demand and also show that drug development can destroy capital.
pitches.business: Novo sells diabetes and obesity medicines. The economic engine is patients treated × duration of treatment × realised net price. Manufacturing capacity and reimbursement determine how much clinical demand becomes revenue. Patents, clinical evidence and production expertise are barriers to entry, but they do not eliminate payer bargaining power or competition.
pitches.thesis: As reconstructed on 27 September 2024, a small position can express the view that additional supply and broader treatment use support several years of earnings growth. The variant hypothesis is that capacity expansion will translate into persistent treatment volumes rather than merely short-lived stocking. It is a hypothesis to test, not evidence that the market has mispriced the shares. Avoid treating the entire obesity market as Novo revenue.
pitches.valuation: Use a five-year revenue bridge separating diabetes and obesity, then patients, adherence and net price. Deduct the manufacturing capital expenditure and working capital required for growth. Cross-check with forward P/E, but normalise the impairment before comparing earnings. Test 10%, 18% and 25% EPS growth with 22×, 28× and 34× exit multiples. These are analyst assumptions, not September consensus. A premium multiple is only defensible if growth survives lower net pricing.
pitches.catalysts: Quarterly treatment-volume disclosure, supply availability, reimbursement decisions and the scheduled CagriSema clinical readout. Do not put the eventual trial result into the initial thesis.
pitches.risks: Lilly competition, compounding, reduced treatment persistence, US price pressure and disappointing trials can reduce both earnings and the multiple simultaneously. An attractive clinical product can still be a poor investment at an excessive price.
pitches.invalidation: Cut exposure if a major readout reduces the expected competitive advantage. Exit if repeated guidance reductions show that the earnings trajectory underlying the purchase no longer holds. Do not average down solely because the share price falls.
pitches.monitor: Net sales versus prescription growth; gross-to-net adjustments; capex/sales; realised price; clinical endpoints and estimands; forward earnings revisions.
pitches.role: 3% starting target. A 50% share-price loss costs approximately 1.5% of starting portfolio capital before correlations. The later journal deliberately includes a losing-thesis review.
pitches.interview: The central question is not whether obesity treatment demand grows. It is how much value remains for shareholders after competition, reimbursement and the cost of supplying that demand.

pitches.name: CME Group
pitches.headline: Own the infrastructure used to transfer macroeconomic risk.
pitches.facts: Q2 2024 revenue was approximately $1.5bn and adjusted diluted EPS was $2.56. Average daily volume was 25.9m contracts. These are operating observations available before portfolio inception, not evidence of a guaranteed volatility hedge.
pitches.business: CME operates futures and options exchanges and clearing infrastructure. Revenue largely follows contract volume × revenue per contract, supplemented by market data and other services. Liquidity attracts liquidity: execution depth, open interest and clearing offsets make it difficult for a new venue to displace the incumbent.
pitches.thesis: The initial case is that uncertainty about inflation, policy rates and refinancing sustains hedging activity across rates, equity indices, FX and commodities. The strongest claim is recurring demand for risk transfer. A weaker claim would be that every market sell-off raises CME earnings. Fee mix, collateral-related income and competition can offset higher headline volumes.
pitches.valuation: Build product-level volumes and revenue per contract, then expenses and distributable cash. Normalise interest-sensitive revenue and separate regular from variable distributions. Test 2%, 6% and 9% annual EPS growth with 20×, 24× and 28× exit P/E. Use total distributions cautiously: a historical special dividend is not a fixed coupon. The model should not capitalise a temporary trading spike forever.
pitches.catalysts: Monthly volume releases, quarterly revenue per contract, changes in open interest and new product adoption. Greater uncertainty around the shape of the rates curve can support demand even if policy rates fall.
pitches.risks: Competitor pricing, exchange regulation, operational outages, cyber incidents, clearing-member stress and lower trading activity. A market infrastructure company remains an equity with valuation risk.
pitches.invalidation: Reassess if volume share and net pricing deteriorate together for two reporting periods or if clearing advantages weaken structurally. A quiet month alone does not invalidate the thesis.
pitches.monitor: Interest-rate ADV; options mix; revenue per contract; market-data growth; expense growth; cash conversion and capital returns.
pitches.role: 4% initial target. It complements directional macro trades but is not counted as a hedge against all portfolio losses.
pitches.interview: I separate the direction of rates from the demand to hedge rates. CME can benefit from activity under different rate paths, although that does not make its share price market-neutral.

pitches.name: Rheinmetall
pitches.headline: Convert a larger defence order book into cash, not just headlines.
pitches.facts: H1 2024 group sales were about €3.8bn, 33% higher than a year earlier. Management confirmed roughly €10bn of 2024 sales and a 14–15% operating margin. Operating free cash flow was negative €19m in the first half.
pitches.business: Rheinmetall supplies ammunition, military vehicles, weapons and electronic systems, alongside its then-existing civil activities. Governments are the principal end customers. Production capacity, security qualifications, long procurement cycles and supply-chain access limit immediate competitive entry.
pitches.thesis: By September 2024, replenishing depleted stocks and improving European military readiness were observable demand drivers. The investable argument is multi-year capacity utilisation and better fixed-cost absorption. Orders are not equivalent to recognised revenue, and framework agreements are not all firm cash receipts. A credible pitch must bridge the order book to deliveries, margins and working capital.
pitches.valuation: Forecast capacity additions, delivery schedules and segment margins. Use a mid-cycle earnings or EBIT multiple and deduct net debt consistently. Test EPS growth of 8%, 18% and 25% with 18×, 24× and 28× exit P/E as a sensitivity, not a target justified by geopolitical headlines. Check customer advances and inventory so apparently strong earnings do not conceal weak free cash flow.
pitches.catalysts: Funded procurement awards, factory commissioning, delivery milestones and contract-level margin evidence. The initial thesis does not assume later German fiscal-policy changes.
pitches.risks: Procurement delays, fixed-price contract inflation, execution failures, political reversals, export restrictions and an already demanding valuation. A ceasefire need not end replenishment, but it can compress the valuation premium.
pitches.invalidation: Reduce if production expansion repeatedly misses milestones or cash conversion deteriorates without a credible timing explanation. A larger backlog alone cannot offset a declining return on invested capital.
pitches.monitor: Firm orders versus frameworks; book-to-bill; deliveries; operating margin; inventory; customer advances and free cash flow.
pitches.role: 3% initial target, capped at 5%. The March 2025 increase is a separate dated decision rather than a claim that later developments were predicted.
pitches.interview: My thesis was a production and cash-conversion thesis. Geopolitics explained customer urgency, but capacity, contract quality and valuation determined the investment.

pitches.name: Schneider Electric
pitches.headline: Electrification demand with an explicit check on the price paid.
pitches.facts: Schneider reported record Q2 2024 revenue of about €9.6bn, with organic growth of 7%. The half-year release was available on 31 July 2024.
pitches.business: Schneider sells energy-management and industrial-automation hardware, software and services. Its installed base, channels, technical integration and customer switching costs support repeat business. Demand comes from buildings, infrastructure, industry and data centres rather than a single end market.
pitches.thesis: The September case is that investment in electrical capacity and efficiency remains necessary across several economic scenarios. Data centres offer incremental demand, but the thesis should survive slower AI investment. The attractive feature is participation in power distribution and management across customers, not a forecast of which AI application wins.
pitches.valuation: Separate energy management from more cyclical automation. Model organic sales, price versus volume, incremental EBITA margin and cash conversion after capex. Test EPS growth of 4%, 9% and 13% with exit multiples of 20×, 25× and 30×. Compare the implied return with a broad equity fund, because buying a good business at a high multiple can be less attractive than the index.
pitches.catalysts: Order conversion, improving automation demand and evidence that data-centre demand adds profitable revenue rather than merely backlog.
pitches.risks: Industrial recession, customer concentration in large projects, supply constraints, expensive acquisitions and elevated expectations. Electrical-equipment exposure can overlap with the technology allocation through common capex customers.
pitches.invalidation: Reassess if organic growth slows while inventories and receivables rise, or if margins require unsustainable price increases. Avoid adding solely on AI-related headlines.
pitches.monitor: Organic growth by segment and geography; orders; backlog conversion; adjusted EBITA; free cash flow; acquisition integration.
pitches.role: 3% initial target. Count the exposure with technology and industrial capex when stress-testing common demand factors.
pitches.interview: This is a way to study the physical infrastructure behind electrification, but I still need evidence that revenue growth produces cash returns above the cost of capital.

pitches.name: Unilever
pitches.headline: A volume-led recovery rather than another round of price increases.
pitches.facts: H1 2024 turnover was €31.1bn. Underlying sales grew 4.1%, comprising 2.6% volume growth and 1.6% pricing. Management expected full-year underlying sales growth within its 3–5% range.
pitches.business: Unilever sells branded everyday products through a broad retail network. Brand investment, distribution and repeat purchasing support its economics. Retailer bargaining power and private labels limit pricing freedom, especially when consumers face pressure on disposable income.
pitches.thesis: After an inflationary period, improving volumes are a more persuasive sign of healthy demand than price-led nominal growth. The September thesis is that focused execution can rebuild volume and protect margins without starving advertising or product development. Its role is to moderate cyclical exposure, not to eliminate equity drawdowns.
pitches.valuation: Build sales through volume, pricing and currency. Stress gross margins against input costs and reinvestment. Test EPS growth of 1%, 5% and 8% with 16×, 20× and 23× exit multiples. Treat restructuring cash outflows as real costs even when excluded from adjusted operating profit. Check dividends against free cash flow rather than accounting earnings alone.
pitches.catalysts: Sustained volume recovery, market-share improvement, margin resilience and progress on the announced business simplification.
pitches.risks: Private-label substitution, emerging-market FX depreciation, weak execution and restructuring costs. The dollar ADR adds a quotation layer; the underlying earnings exposure remains international.
pitches.invalidation: Reduce if volume improves only through promotions that erode cash margins, or if cost cutting damages brand investment and market share.
pitches.monitor: Underlying volume and price growth; gross margin; brand investment; cash conversion; geographic currency effects.
pitches.role: 2% initial target. A small defensive equity allocation alongside the broad index core.
pitches.interview: I prefer to see consumers buying more units, not only paying higher prices. The investment case needs volume, margins and reinvestment to improve together.

pitches.name: Microsoft
pitches.headline: A strong franchise already present in the index core.
pitches.facts: Microsoft published its FY2024 Q4 results on 30 July 2024. The release and segment disclosures allow an investor to distinguish enterprise subscriptions, Azure and other businesses instead of treating all revenue as AI revenue.
pitches.business: Subscriptions, cloud consumption and enterprise distribution create recurring revenue and switching costs. Azure requires substantial infrastructure investment. Software margins and cloud infrastructure economics should be modelled separately.
pitches.thesis: As of September 2024, an attractive business case centres on installed enterprise relationships and cloud adoption. The contested question is whether incremental AI monetisation earns sufficient returns on new capital. A large addressable market does not establish profitable unit economics. The portfolio already owns Microsoft indirectly through global and US indices, so a direct position needs a genuinely distinct expected-return case.
pitches.valuation: Build the cloud segment with consumption growth, operating margin, capex and subsequent depreciation. Model mature software separately. Cross-check with free-cash-flow yield and reverse-DCF assumptions. In the illustrative multiple sensitivity, use EPS growth of 5%, 12% and 17%, with 24×, 30× and 35× exit P/E. Growth and valuation assumptions must not both be optimistic by default.
pitches.catalysts: Azure growth relative to investment, paid Copilot adoption and evidence that capacity additions monetise at attractive margins.
pitches.risks: AI capex oversupply, competitive pricing, regulatory intervention, cyber incidents and concentration in the same US growth factor already held through indices.
pitches.invalidation: Do not initiate if the required future cash-flow growth exceeds plausible customer adoption. Reassess any future position if rising capex persistently fails to improve revenue and cash generation.
pitches.monitor: Cloud consumption; commercial bookings; capex and depreciation; cash conversion; revenue per user; index look-through exposure.
pitches.role: Watchlist, 0% direct starting weight. Studying a company does not oblige the portfolio to own it.
pitches.interview: The best expression of conviction can be declining to add a stock already heavily represented in the benchmark until valuation offers a margin of safety.

pitches.name: Shell
pitches.headline: Value cash distributions across the cycle, not at one oil price.
pitches.facts: Shell reported Q2 2024 adjusted earnings of approximately $6.3bn. The company results distinguish upstream, integrated gas, refining and other activities, which respond differently to commodity prices.
pitches.business: Shell produces and markets oil and gas, liquefies and trades LNG, and operates downstream businesses. Asset quality, operating costs, capital discipline and trading capability matter, but realised commodity prices dominate much of the earnings cycle.
pitches.thesis: The reconstructed September watchlist case is disciplined capital allocation and a diversified LNG franchise. The proposed portfolio already has an oil-futures proxy, so owning Shell would introduce both overlapping energy risk and separate corporate execution risk. A cheap headline earnings multiple may simply reflect unsustainably high cycle earnings.
pitches.valuation: Use a commodity-price deck with oil, gas and refining sensitivities. Estimate sustaining capex before growth capex, then dividends and buybacks from remaining free cash flow. Test mid-cycle EPS growth of −5%, 2% and 6% with 7×, 9× and 11× exit P/E. These simplified cases are secondary to an asset-level cash-flow model. Buybacks only create value when the repurchase price is sensible.
pitches.catalysts: Lower controllable costs, project start-ups, cash generation through a weaker commodity environment and evidence that capital returns do not rely on higher leverage.
pitches.risks: Oil and gas price falls, project overruns, fiscal changes, environmental liabilities and expensive strategic reversals. Dividends and buybacks can be cut.
pitches.invalidation: Reject initiation if distributions require borrowing under the mid-cycle price case. Reduce if management repeatedly raises spending without improving expected returns.
pitches.monitor: Organic free cash flow; net debt; sustaining capex; LNG volumes; realised prices and refining margins.
pitches.role: Watchlist. Any future purchase should be assessed together with BNO and other cyclical exposures.
pitches.interview: I would not pitch an energy major from its P/E alone. I want to know what is left for shareholders after maintaining production at a normal commodity price.

pitches.name: Rio Tinto
pitches.headline: Copper optionality inside an iron-ore-sensitive cash generator.
pitches.facts: Rio Tinto reported approximately $12.1bn of underlying EBITDA for H1 2024. The interim report provides commodity sensitivities and segment information needed to avoid treating the company as a pure copper investment.
pitches.business: Mining economics combine commodity prices, ore quality, recovery rates, throughput, freight, energy and sustaining investment. Large established assets can have cost advantages, but depletion requires recurring capital expenditure.
pitches.thesis: The September watchlist thesis balances low-cost assets and prospective copper growth against exposure to Chinese steel demand through iron ore. Copper demand from electrification is plausible, but its timing and price effect are uncertain. A position should be sized on the earnings mix that exists, not only on the mix an investor hopes will exist later.
pitches.valuation: Use separate iron ore, copper and aluminium price assumptions. Stress EBITDA using disclosed sensitivities, then account for tax, capex and debt. Test EPS growth of −6%, 2% and 7% with 7×, 9× and 11× exit P/E only as a secondary check. A single-year dividend yield can mislead when payout follows volatile earnings.
pitches.catalysts: Operational delivery at growth projects, cost control, improved commodity demand and stronger cash conversion.
pitches.risks: China property weakness, falling iron ore prices, operational disruptions, project overruns, political exposure and environmental liabilities. Commodity and currency effects interact.
pitches.invalidation: Avoid initiation if attractive valuation requires a rapid Chinese demand recovery. Reassess if growth projects consume significantly more capital without a corresponding return improvement.
pitches.monitor: Iron ore shipments and realised prices; unit costs; copper output; project capex; leverage and dividend coverage.
pitches.role: Watchlist. Compare with direct copper exposure before adding another cyclical asset.
pitches.interview: A company can have an exciting copper story and still trade predominantly on iron ore. I size risk from current cash-flow drivers.

pitches.name: LVMH
pitches.headline: Exceptional brands still face cyclical demand and valuation risk.
pitches.facts: LVMH reported H1 2024 revenue of approximately €41.7bn. Its July release described the prevailing economic and geopolitical uncertainty. The initial analysis therefore cannot assume an imminent consumer recovery.
pitches.business: The group owns luxury houses across fashion, leather goods, wines and spirits, jewellery, perfumes and retail. Brand desirability, controlled distribution and scarcity support pricing, but profitability varies materially between divisions.
pitches.thesis: The September case for studying LVMH is that long-lived brands can retain pricing power over a cycle. The case against immediate purchase is uncertainty around aspirational consumption and Chinese demand. A lower price is not enough: separate a temporary slowdown from deteriorating brand demand or an exhausted pricing strategy.
pitches.valuation: Build segment-level organic sales and margins. Fashion and leather goods should not share the same multiple as all other divisions without justification. Test EPS growth of −2%, 6% and 11% with 18×, 24× and 28× exit P/E. Require a return that compensates for both cyclical earnings risk and potential multiple compression.
pitches.catalysts: Stabilising organic growth, sustained full-price sell-through, tourism spending and evidence that weaker demand does not require broad discounting.
pitches.risks: China concentration, currency shifts, travel disruption, brand fatigue, excess inventory and a loss of exclusivity. High gross margins do not remove operating leverage.
pitches.invalidation: Do not initiate while the thesis rests solely on a rapid demand rebound. Reassess after persistent inventory accumulation or a weakening brand price architecture.
pitches.monitor: Organic revenue by division; regional customer demand; inventory; store productivity; operating margin and cash conversion.
pitches.role: Watchlist. A consumer exposure distinct from Unilever, with much greater discretionary demand sensitivity.
pitches.interview: The brand is an asset, but the investment return still depends on the cycle and the expectations embedded in the purchase price.

pitches.name: Prologis
pitches.headline: Rental growth must outrun financing costs and cap-rate risk.
pitches.facts: Prologis reported Q2 2024 core FFO per diluted share of $1.34. Its supplemental disclosures allow analysis of occupancy, rent changes, development and financing. Core FFO is a non-GAAP metric and is not the same as free cash available after recurring property investment.
pitches.business: Prologis owns and develops logistics properties and earns fees from investment partnerships. Location, customer networks and scale matter. Lease renewals can move rents toward market levels, while interest costs and property yields affect equity value.
pitches.thesis: The reconstructed September watchlist case is an embedded opportunity to reset older leases, coupled with a potential easing in financing conditions. The critical distinction is that central-bank cuts do not mechanically lower long-term property discount rates. A slowing economy can reduce tenant demand at the same time.
pitches.valuation: Use NAV with explicit stabilised NOI and cap rates, then reconcile debt and diluted shares. Cross-check price/core FFO and adjusted cash flow after recurring capex. Test per-share growth of 0%, 5% and 9% with 17×, 21× and 25× exit multiples of normalised recurring FFO. Do not compare FFO multiples directly with operating-company P/E.
pitches.catalysts: Lease renewals, occupancy stabilisation, development leasing and debt refinancing on acceptable terms.
pitches.risks: Logistics oversupply, tenant weakness, refinancing risk, higher cap rates and development commitments. Listed property can behave like cyclical equity during stress.
pitches.invalidation: Reject the case if positive rent resets cannot offset occupancy losses and higher financing costs, or if NAV depends on cap-rate compression.
pitches.monitor: Cash same-store NOI; occupancy; net effective rent changes; debt maturities; fixed-rate share of debt; development yields.
pitches.role: Watchlist. Adds real-estate research without pretending that listed REITs are a substitute for the sovereign-bond sleeve.
pitches.interview: I value the property cash flows and financing separately. A rate-cut story is incomplete unless the rental and cap-rate assumptions also make sense.

journal.title: Establish the diversified research portfolio
journal.changes: Establish the initial 100% funded allocation, including a 4% cash target.
journal.why: September easing by the Federal Reserve and ECB makes the path of inflation and growth central to the portfolio. A balanced starting point avoids requiring one macro forecast to be correct. The global index already contains US and European equities: the additional funds are deliberate regional tilts, not extra independent diversification.
journal.evidence: The Fed cut its target range to 4.75–5.00% on 18 September. The ECB lowered its deposit rate to 3.50% in September. The August carry unwind was already documented by the BIS.
journal.alternative: A single global equity fund plus short sovereign bonds would be simpler. The extra sleeves exist to develop and test explicit macro and company theses, with strict position limits.
journal.risk: Unhedged dollar bond exposure can dominate duration P&L in EUR. Several asset classes may fall together. A global recession stress must include equities, industrial commodities, carry and crypto.
journal.invalidate: Rebalance when a documented thesis breaks or risk limits are exceeded. Do not trade on every macro headline.
journal.implementation: Initial purchase at 30 September closing references, after the 27 September information cutoff. This is a closing-price simulation with modelled costs, not reconstructed broker fills. This expanded edition adds monthly monitoring and broader asset-class target reviews. Those rules were specified in September 2026, not prospectively in 2024.

journal.title: 2024-10 · Review and retain the allocation
journal.why: Preserve the documented targets and avoid paying costs for small weight changes. A scheduled review is not a requirement to trade.
journal.evidence: Review at 2024-10-31 close. NAV €101,007.61; cash 3.72%; drawdown -2.34%. No drift-band or concentration trigger breached.
journal.alternative: Do nothing and allow winners and losers to keep changing the portfolio. Alternatively, reset every month regardless of drift; that increases turnover.
journal.risk: Rebalancing may sell a continuing winner or add to a continuing loser. Transaction costs and taxes can outweigh a small diversification benefit.
journal.invalidate: Escalate material company information to a separate thesis review. The generic drift rule must not substitute for reassessing a broken thesis.
journal.implementation: No transaction. Keep units unchanged and continue monitoring.

journal.title: 2024-11 · Rebalance weights after drift
journal.changes: Restore the existing target allocation after the documented drift or risk trigger.
journal.why: Return to the approved risk budget after material price-driven drift. This is allocation maintenance, not a new price forecast.
journal.evidence: Review at 2024-11-29 close. NAV €107,737.84; cash 3.48%; drawdown -0.06%. Triggers: BTC-USD: actual 3.02%, target 2.00%.
journal.alternative: Do nothing and allow winners and losers to keep changing the portfolio. Alternatively, reset every month regardless of drift; that increases turnover.
journal.risk: Rebalancing may sell a continuing winner or add to a continuing loser. Transaction costs and taxes can outweigh a small diversification benefit.
journal.invalidate: Escalate material company information to a separate thesis review. The generic drift rule must not substitute for reassessing a broken thesis.
journal.implementation: Execute at the next common-market close. Reset the funded book to its documented targets, charging every side.

journal.title: Reduce duration after the Fed’s projection reset
journal.why: A higher expected policy path reduces confidence in a rapid sequence of cuts. Move two percentage points from intermediate Treasuries into shorter maturities, retaining sovereign exposure and limiting reliance on one disinflation forecast.
journal.evidence: The December median projection for the end-2025 policy rate was 3.9%, versus 3.4% in the September projection. These are policymakers’ conditional assessments, not market forward rates.
journal.alternative: Keep the original duration for recession protection; that is reasonable if weaker activity dominates inflation persistence.
journal.risk: Selling duration after a repricing can crystallise a loss and miss a rally. USD translation is unchanged.
journal.invalidate: Add duration only after a fresh US growth/inflation review and a comparison with the yield already available.
journal.implementation: Apply the documented target revision at the following eligible common-market closing references. Rebalance all funded sleeves; deduct 25 bp per side, 50 bp for crypto. This is a retrospective scenario choice, not a contemporaneous order.

journal.title: Reduce Novo after the clinical readout
journal.why: The original position required clinical differentiation to help defend future growth. The REDEFINE 1 result supports efficacy but warrants a lower confidence level in the more optimistic differentiation case. Reduce risk before deciding whether the lower share price is attractive.
journal.evidence: The company reported 22.7% weight loss under the treatment-adherence estimand. Distinguish this from outcomes regardless of treatment adherence. Do not describe a stock-price reaction as proof that the medicine does not work.
journal.alternative: Hold the full position and argue that manufacturing and reimbursement matter more than the next-generation product. The smaller position recognises that possibility while reducing the cost of being wrong.
journal.risk: The reduced allocation can miss a rebound. Selling after news absorbs the gap; the simulation cannot use the pre-announcement price.
journal.invalidate: Restore exposure only after a refreshed valuation and evidence of competitive differentiation. Further deterioration in commercial guidance would trigger another review.
journal.implementation: Next trading-session close, 23 December. All funded sleeves reset to the stated target weights on this rebalance date; incidental drift trades are included in costs.

journal.title: Cut the proposed yen-funded carry risk budget
journal.changes: Indicative long AUD/JPY notional 3% → 1.5%; long MXN/JPY 2% → 0%. No funded-book trade.
journal.why: The Bank of Japan tightening increases the funding cost and raises the possibility of yen appreciation. The Mexican peso leg adds risk that can compound with global equity losses. Preserve an FX research programme but remove the higher-risk leg pending a full re-underwriting.
journal.evidence: The BoJ raised its overnight-rate guideline to around 0.5% on 24 January. The August 2024 unwind already demonstrated that carry can lose much more on the exchange rate than it earns in interest.
journal.alternative: Keep both positions on the basis that the yield differential remains positive. This ignores that a positive differential is compensation for risk, not a guarantee of total return.
journal.risk: A stronger risk-on environment can make this conservative reduction underperform. Funding-rate changes alone are insufficient to determine an FX trade.
journal.invalidate: Reopen only with quoted forwards, realistic financing spreads, volatility sizing and a clear reason the expected depreciation is smaller than the carry.
journal.implementation: Research-overlay decision only. No historical FX P&L is included without actual forward points or a complete funding-rate series. The reserve remains EUR cash.

journal.title: Reduce the AUD/JPY research budget after the RBA cut
journal.changes: Indicative AUD/JPY research budget 1.5% → 1.0%; MXN/JPY remains 0%. Funded portfolio unchanged.
journal.why: The RBA easing narrows the illustrative investment-versus-funding differential after the BoJ tightening. Lower the proposed AUD/JPY notional budget from 1.5% to 1%; retain zero MXN/JPY. This is a proposed overlay, not a booked forward position.
journal.evidence: The RBA reduced the cash-rate target by 25 bp to 4.10%. A policy differential is not an executable forward quote.
journal.alternative: Maintain the small research allocation on the view that AUD appreciation could dominate the narrower carry.
journal.risk: A stronger Australian dollar could reward the unchanged position; narrower carry alone is not sufficient to forecast FX.
journal.invalidate: Proceed only after obtaining executable forwards, both funding curves, collateral terms and a EUR risk translation.
journal.implementation: No funded transaction or FX-overlay P&L. Track this as a dated research-budget decision.

journal.title: Raise Rheinmetall’s permitted target to 4%
journal.why: The updated operating outlook supports a larger, but still bounded, allocation. The increase is justified by delivery and revenue expectations rather than an assumption that defence shares must rise indefinitely. The original exposure was already present before this update.
journal.evidence: In the FY2024 results release, management guided to 25–30% group sales growth in 2025 after roughly €9.8bn of 2024 sales.
journal.alternative: Hold at 3% and wait for free-cash-flow evidence. That remains reasonable: higher expected sales need more working capital and may already be reflected in valuation.
journal.risk: The incremental 1% weight increases exposure to execution, political and valuation risk. A 40% stock drawdown would cost about 1.6% of NAV at the 4% target.

journal.title: Freeze the reconstruction and begin forward paper decisions
journal.changes: No automatic trade. Preserve the final reconstructed holdings and cash as the opening forward book.
journal.why: Publish this expanded retrospective scenario as a distinct edition and preserve the earlier one. The forward paper book starts from the new handover only after explicit reconciliation; existing browser records are retained.
journal.evidence: The performance snapshot uses completed reference bars through 18 September 2026. No 21 September intraday quote is treated as a final closing price.
journal.alternative: Start a separate €100,000 live paper book. That is useful for a clean forward record, but it must not be spliced into the historical return series as if no capital flow occurred.
journal.risk: Retrospective security selection and decision selection still contain hindsight. Using dated sources reduces factual look-ahead but does not turn this into an unbiased or prospectively traded track record.

journal.implementation: The trading desk records new decisions, transactions and marks locally. Export a backup after each session. It does not submit real-money orders or provide automatic market feeds.

assets.name: Index equities
assets.mechanism: Own a diversified claim on corporate earnings through a fund. Return comes from cash distributions, per-share earnings growth and changes in valuation. A USD quotation does not mean all underlying economic exposure is to the dollar.
assets.implementation: The funded simulation uses VT (global all-cap), VOO (US large-cap tilt) and IEUR (Europe tilt). These are US-listed research proxies, not an assertion of retail availability in France. Before a real implementation, map exposures to suitable UCITS funds and check the share class, domicile, fees and distribution treatment.
assets.thesis: Keep most equity capital diversified because confidence in individual companies is weaker than the evidence for diversification. The extra US and Europe funds deliberately overlap VT. Evaluate look-through concentration rather than counting tickers.
assets.risk: A global recession can lower earnings and valuation together. Regional tilts and individual stocks can increase common factor exposure. Stock and fund domicile alone do not measure revenue exposure.
assets.math: EUR total return = (1 + local total return) × (FX at end / FX at start) − 1, where FX is EUR per unit of quotation currency.
assets.rule: 50% starting index allocation; single-stock sleeve 15%; 5% individual-stock cap at reviews. These are chosen governance limits, not statistically optimal weights.

assets.name: Rates & sovereign bonds
assets.mechanism: A bond pays contractual cash flows. Price responds to the discount curve, inflation expectations and term premium. A Treasury fund continually rolls its portfolio, so it has no fixed maturity payoff like an individual bond held to maturity.
assets.implementation: IEF is the 7–10-year US Treasury proxy and SHY the 1–3-year proxy. Both are unhedged in EUR in this reconstruction. The June 2025 switch reduces interest-rate sensitivity. No swaps or futures are represented by a cash-fund return.
assets.thesis: Starting yields and potential disinflation can make sovereign duration useful. However, a policy cut already priced into forwards is not free alpha, and a higher term premium can raise long yields despite cuts.
assets.risk: Duration, curve shape, dollar translation and inflation. Nominal government debt is not an inflation hedge. FX volatility may exceed the rates return for a EUR investor.
assets.math: Approximate price change ≈ −modified duration × Δyield + 0.5 × convexity × (Δyield)². DV01 ≈ market value × modified duration × 0.0001. Coupon income and roll-down are separate.
assets.rule: 18% Treasury sleeve. Illustrative durations of 7.2 and 1.8 years imply starting portfolio DV01 ≈ €8.50 per bp on €100,000, before FX; these are stress assumptions, not retrieved historical fund durations.

assets.name: FX carry: AUD/JPY and MXN/JPY
assets.mechanism: Borrow or sell a low-yield currency and hold a higher-yield currency. A positive interest differential can be overwhelmed by depreciation of the long currency. Carry often behaves like selling crash insurance when many investors hold the same trade.
assets.implementation: Research overlays start with 3% AUD/JPY and 2% MXN/JPY indicative notional against a 4% EUR cash reserve. They are proposals, not executed historical positions. To trade them, record spot and forward bid/ask quotes, maturity, notional, both legs, collateral currency and mark-to-market. The historical performance excludes FX-overlay profits and losses.
assets.thesis: In September 2024, the August unwind made aggressive yen-funded leverage hard to defend. A small developed-market leg and an even more tightly controlled emerging-market leg provide a research framework. The January 2025 memo reduces this budget after BoJ tightening.
assets.risk: Yen appreciation, global deleveraging, Mexican political and trade risk, funding spreads, collateral calls and stop slippage. Two pairs funded in JPY are not independent trades.
assets.math: For S quoted as JPY per AUD, covered-interest parity gives F = S × (1 + rJPY × T) / (1 + rAUD × T). A long-AUD forward payoff at maturity is N_AUD × (S_T − F) JPY. Convert the payoff to EUR. Do not add interest carry again to a forward payoff.
assets.rule: Indicative combined notional ≤5% of NAV, no portfolio borrowing. A 15% adverse move on 5% notional costs about 0.75% NAV before funding and slippage. Stop levels are monitoring triggers, not guaranteed fills.

assets.name: Gold
assets.mechanism: Gold has no contractual cash flow. Returns depend on changes in the price investors pay for its scarcity, liquidity and perceived monetary role, less holding costs.
assets.implementation: GLD is the physical-gold research proxy. Its adjusted market-price return includes fund-level expenses embedded in price. It is not the return of a gold miner or a promise of direct access to allocated bars.
assets.thesis: A small allocation can diversify some monetary and geopolitical scenarios. It is not justified by claiming that gold reliably tracks monthly consumer-price inflation.
assets.risk: Rising real yields, dollar effects, valuation reversal, no income and periods of positive correlation with other risky assets.
assets.math: EUR gold return combines the USD gold move and dollar translation. Storage and product fees reduce the investable return.
assets.rule: 6% initial target. No tactical increase based solely on recent price strength.

assets.name: Silver
assets.mechanism: Silver combines investment demand with industrial demand. It can behave differently from gold because manufacturing demand and supply conditions matter.
assets.implementation: SLV is a physical-silver price proxy. Analyse trust structure and embedded costs separately from the metal thesis.
assets.thesis: A 2% research allocation allows exposure to industrial and monetary demand without pretending it is equivalent to the gold sleeve.
assets.risk: Higher volatility, weaker liquidity in stress and sensitivity to an industrial slowdown. Gold and silver are not independent safe-haven positions.
assets.math: A 40% loss in silver at a 2% starting weight reduces initial portfolio capital by roughly 0.8%, before other moves.
assets.rule: 2% starting target. Review the combined precious-metals exposure rather than raising both positions independently.

assets.name: Copper
assets.mechanism: Copper is consumed in electrical networks, construction and manufacturing. Spot prices respond to supply, inventories and marginal demand. A futures investment also responds to the shape of the futures curve.
assets.implementation: CPER is the copper-futures fund proxy. Use its actual adjusted return rather than substituting the spot copper price. Embedded roll mechanics and fund expenses matter.
assets.thesis: Electrification supports a long-run demand hypothesis, but China, the business cycle and new supply can dominate near-term returns. The 1% allocation recognises this uncertainty.
assets.risk: Industrial recession, supply expansion, substitution, inventory cycles and negative roll yield. The portfolio already has indirect electrification exposure through Schneider.
assets.math: Collateralised futures return is approximately spot-price change + roll return + collateral return − implementation costs. This decomposition is explanatory, not an exact daily identity for every fund.
assets.rule: 1% target; stress jointly with industrial equities. Do not extrapolate a demand narrative directly into a price forecast.

assets.name: Brent oil
assets.mechanism: Oil prices reflect marginal supply and demand, inventories, spare capacity and geopolitical disruptions. The futures curve changes the return from owning exposure over time.
assets.implementation: BNO is a Brent-futures proxy. It is a fund return, not a constant holding of spot barrels. Its roll methodology and embedded expenses distinguish it from Shell equity.
assets.thesis: A small allocation provides exposure to supply-shock scenarios. It can lose money in a recession even if geopolitical risk remains elevated.
assets.risk: Demand destruction, supply increases, OPEC decisions, contango and sharp gap moves. Energy equities add corporate risks and are not interchangeable with futures.
assets.math: A rising spot price can coexist with a disappointing futures-fund return if roll and expenses are adverse.
assets.rule: 1% target; analyse with Shell and broader cyclical risk if a future stock purchase is proposed.

assets.name: Bitcoin
assets.mechanism: Bitcoin is a scarce digital bearer asset with no contractual cash flow. Price reflects demand for the network and asset, liquidity and investor expectations.
assets.implementation: BTC-USD is a spot reference series. It excludes exchange-specific spreads, custody events and execution venue risk. The model deducts an assumed trading cost but does not include lending or staking income.
assets.thesis: A small, explicitly speculative allocation tests an adoption and scarcity thesis without requiring crypto to behave as a stable inflation hedge.
assets.risk: Large drawdowns, changing correlations, custody failures, regulatory restrictions and weekend liquidity. Historical return patterns are not evidence of an intrinsic value floor.
assets.math: At a 2% weight, an 80% price decline costs about 1.6% of initial capital before rebalancing effects.
assets.rule: 2% BTC plus 1% ETH initially. No leverage, yield farming or assumed risk-free lending. Review the combined crypto sleeve against a 5% cap.

assets.name: Ethereum
assets.mechanism: Ethereum supports transaction execution and applications. ETH economics involve demand for block space, issuance, fee burning and validator incentives. Token value capture is distinct from application usage.
assets.implementation: ETH-USD is an unstaked spot reference. Staking income is excluded because it requires a separate implementation, fees and risk accounting.
assets.thesis: The 1% position tests demand for programmable settlement, while recognising that network activity does not automatically create proportional tokenholder returns.
assets.risk: Technology failures, competing networks, scaling-related fee changes, custody and regulatory risk. BTC and ETH share substantial crypto-market exposure.
assets.math: Combine BTC and ETH when measuring crypto risk. Two tokens do not create two independent asset classes.
assets.rule: 1% initial target. Do not increase merely because transaction counts rise; investigate fee economics and value capture.

assets.name: EUR cash & collateral
assets.mechanism: Cash funds near-term decisions and collateral requirements. Its value is stable in the portfolio base currency, but inflation erodes purchasing power.
assets.implementation: The historical simulation assumes zero interest on EUR cash. This deliberately avoids inventing a deposit rate. Treasury-fund distributions are already handled inside their adjusted-price series.
assets.thesis: A reserve supports patient decisions and reduces the need to sell risky assets under pressure. It is an explicit allocation, not an unexplained balancing item.
assets.risk: Opportunity cost, inflation and counterparty exposure in a real implementation. Collateral is not additional investment capital.
assets.math: NAV = funded asset values + cash. Derivative notionals are disclosed separately and must never be added to NAV as if they were assets.
assets.rule: 4% initial cash, changed only by dated target decisions and trading costs. FX overlay P&L remains excluded until a properly priced implementation exists.

Use a simple index core, bounded discretionary weights and a transparent benchmark.

carry
Carry strategies can exhibit negative skew and sharp losses when funding liquidity deteriorates.
Cap FX notional, aggregate common funding-currency exposure and stress large spot moves.
A historical premium is not an arbitrage or a forecast for a specific currency pair.
commodities
Historical diversified collateralised commodity futures have distinct inflation and business-cycle properties.
Include small commodity sleeves and account for roll and collateral returns.
Evidence for a diversified futures basket does not directly validate a concentrated copper or oil trade.
gold
Gold is an unreliable short-horizon inflation hedge and its real price can vary substantially.
Use a modest diversifier allocation and avoid a mechanical inflation hedge claim.
The research does not give a reliable short-term price target.
crypto
Crypto return drivers differ from traditional asset returns in the studied sample.
Keep a separate small speculative budget and avoid assuming stable stock or gold correlations.
The early sample is short and market structure changes; historical patterns may not persist.
trend
The study documents time-series momentum across liquid futures markets.
Keep a pre-specified trend overlay as a possible future research project, with costs and out-of-sample testing.
No trend signal is secretly applied to this historical portfolio. A reading list is not an implemented strategy.
